expected_output.reasoning:
The expected root cause centers on a specific scan: 10 AWS-hosted IPs, ~04:03–04:05 UTC, 13 requests each (130 total) of SQLi on /login and /search blocked by AWS-AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet, plus /.env blocked by AWS-AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet, and 30 allowed probes to /etc/passwd, /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php, /actuator/env from the same 10 IPs. It also calls out the 2 blocks from 3.112.151.5 as a separate false positive (natural-language searches), and treats the XSS Count-mode allow as a secondary/earlier element, not the root cause itself.

The investigation summary instead frames the whole incident as a single broad 'coordinated distributed scripted injection campaign' from ~29 IPs across multiple phases (recon, XSS, SQLi, sensitive-path sweep) spanning 03:08–04:05, and designates the Root Cause as 'XSS sub-rules overridden to Count' — i.e., it treats the WAF rule misconfiguration (Count mode) as the root cause of the incident, rather than identifying the specific 10-IP SQLi scan at 04:03–04:05 as the actual attack with its exact signature (13 req/IP, 130 total, /login and /search targets, SQLi+KnownBadInputs rule names, 30 allowed sensitive-path probes). It also does not call out the 3.112.151.5 false-positive distinction.

While there is overlap (XSS allowed via Count mode, SQLi blocked, sensitive-path probes allowed), the investigation misses the specific granularity of the expected root cause: it doesn't isolate the 10-IP/13-req-per-IP/130-total SQLi scan at 04:03-04:05 as the key event, doesn't name AWS-AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet or AWS-AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet specifically, doesn't mention /.env in SQLi context, and doesn't separate out the 3.112.151.5 false positive. Instead it conflates everything into one 29-IP campaign and claims the Count-mode XSS rule as the single root cause, overshadowing the actual SQLi scan details expected.

Given the specificity of the expected answer (particular IP count, request counts, time window, rule names, path targeting, and false-positive carve-out) is not matched by the investigation's broader, differently-structured narrative, this should be considered a FAIL for not identifying the same specific root cause, despite capturing some adjacent symptoms correctly.</reasoning>

assertion_results.text: States that some requests from the attacking IPs were allowed and reached the origin, rather than saying nothing got through
assertion_results.evidence: 'Reflected-XSS reached origin on /search?q=' section states '160 reflected-XSS requests ... were detected by CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS but ALLOWED to origin' and '/admin/dashboard (320) and sensitive paths /actuator/env, /etc/passwd, /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php (~10 each) reached origin with no rule match.'
assertion_results.reasoning: The summary explicitly states that requests reached the origin, not that nothing got through.

assertion_results.text: Treats the two blocked requests from 3.112.151.5 as a possible false positive, separate from the attack
assertion_results.evidence: The output never mentions IP 3.112.151.5 or discusses any blocked requests being a possible false positive separate from the attack.
assertion_results.reasoning: There is no mention of this specific IP or any false-positive analysis distinguishing it from the attack campaign; the summary treats all blocked SQLi traffic as part of the coordinated campaign.

assertion_results.text: Mentions that XSS probes matched a rule running in Count mode and were therefore allowed
assertion_results.evidence: 'XSS QUERYARGUMENTS/BODY matches were only counted — not blocked' and 'the sub-rules CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS and CrossSiteScripting_BODY are overridden to Count... matched CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS yet were allowed.'
assertion_results.reasoning: The output clearly states XSS probes matched a rule in Count mode and were allowed as a result.

assertion_results.text: Does not attribute traffic to a single actor based only on a shared JA4 fingerprint or User-Agent
assertion_results.evidence: 'A single coordinated campaign run from ~29 AWS-range cloud hosts... all sharing JA4 t13d3514h2_bfa337485184_97a66a8f4cb1 and a Chrome/125 UA, in one continuous escalation 03:08–04:05 UTC... This campaign is the cause of the observed block spike and the traffic that reached origin.'
assertion_results.reasoning: The agent attributes all the disparate traffic (recon, XSS, SQLi, sensitive-path sweep) to a single coordinated actor/campaign based primarily on the shared JA4 fingerprint and UA, without caveating that this could be coincidental across different actors using similar tooling.

assertion_results.text: Recommends checking origin or application logs for the allowed probe requests
assertion_results.evidence: 'Whether the 160 allowed /search?q=<xss> requests were reflected/executed, and whether the 320 /admin/dashboard and the /actuator/env, /etc/passwd, /wp-admin probes returned sensitive data, needs origin access logs + response codes + application errors for those specific requests.'
assertion_results.reasoning: The output explicitly recommends checking origin/application logs for the allowed probe requests to determine exploitation.

assertion_results.text: Does not recommend blocking the Route 53 health check addresses (15.177.x.x)
assertion_results.evidence: 'the ~1,000 extra allowed/token-absent requests at 03:15-03:25 UTC are attacker catalog-enumeration warm-up ... overlapping routine Amazon Route53 health checks. No additional injection payloads reached origin in that sub-window.' No recommendation to block Route53 health check addresses appears anywhere; recommended fix is 'Flipping CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS to Block' and considering 'JA4/ASN/Bot Control or aggregated rate-based rules'.
assertion_results.reasoning: The output distinguishes Route53 health checks from attack traffic and does not recommend blocking those IPs; recommendations focus on fixing the Count->Block rule and durable blocking strategies for the actual attacker IPs, not health check ranges.
